patient_information: A 32-year-old man from Malawi with a past medical history unremarkable except for an episode of a blistering and painful skin lesion 3 years previously that affected the right side of his abdomen around the level of the umbilicus, which healed spontaneously after several weeks. He was found to be HIV positive.
chief_complaint: Pain in his right upper abdomen and a feeling of faintness, especially when standing up and walking, for 1 month.
history_of_present_illness: One month prior to presentation, he began to experience a feeling of fullness in his upper abdomen. In the week before admission, he developed pain in the right upper abdomen that was particularly apparent when sleeping on his right side. He had recently started to feel breathless on lying down and feels faint, especially on standing up.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a young African man from Malawi. A previous attack of herpes zoster 3 years prior was a strong pointer to HIV infection. In Africa, tuberculosis is the most common cause of pericardial effusion, and there is a strong association between tuberculosis and HIV infection in central and southern Africa.
vitals: Pulse is regular at 130bpm. Pulsus paradoxus measured at 15 mmHg. Blood pressure in the supine position is 90/60 mm Hg.
physical_exam: He is thin and slightly breathless in the supine position. The jugular venous pulse is difficult to visualize but appears elevated. The apex beat is impalpable. The heart sounds are quiet but audible; no triple rhythm and no heart murmurs are heard. Auscultation of the chest is normal. There is an enlarged tender palpable liver measured at 8 cm below the right costal junction and evidence of mild peripheral oedema of the legs and sacral area.
labs_and_diagnostics: Haemoglobin 10.5g/dL; WBC 9.8 G/L (4–10). Chest radiography showed an enlarged globular heart with clear lung fields. An HIV test was carried out and found to be positive. An ultrasound of the heart was indicated and likely would show pericardial fluid and fibrous strands suggestive of tuberculosis. Diagnostic pericardial aspiration is usually unhelpful in the district hospital setting due to fluid being often bloodstained and acid-fast bacilli rarely visualized, but the Xpert MTB/RIF assay can provide a confirmed diagnosis of TB within 2 hours.
differential_diagnosis: Based on the clinical history, examination, and chest radiograph findings, the most likely pathology is pericardial tamponade caused by a large pericardial effusion. The cardiovascular manifestations of tachycardia, pulsus paradoxus, hypotension, impalpable apex beat, raised jugular venous pressure, and quiet heart sounds are indicative of pericardial effusion. The presence of syncope, pulsus paradoxus, and hypotension are signs of cardiac tamponade. In Africa, common causes of pericardial effusion include tuberculosis, other bacterial infections, malignancy, and HIV-related Kaposi's sarcoma. The previous attack of herpes zoster strongly points to HIV infection, making HIV-associated tuberculosis the most likely diagnosis.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient underwent therapeutic pericardial aspiration, and 500 mL of bloodstained pericardial fluid were aspirated, resulting in an immediate increase in blood pressure to 120/80 mmHg. He was started on standard first-line antituberculous treatment with rifampicin (R), isoniazid (H), pyrazinamide (Z), and ethambutol (E), along with prednisolone at a dose of 60 mg daily. The patient received a full 6-month course of antituberculous treatment, consisting of a 2-month initial phase of four drugs (2RHZE) and a 4-month continuation phase of two drugs (4RH). Prednisolone was administered in tapering doses for ten weeks. Antiretroviral therapy was started at 4 weeks after commencing antituberculous treatment, and he made a full and uneventful recovery.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is HIV-associated tuberculous pericardial tamponade. This is supported by the clinical presentation of right upper abdominal pain, breathlessness, and syncope, along with physical exam findings of cardiac decompensation and a chest radiograph showing an enlarged globular cardiac silhouette. The history of a previous herpes zoster lesion strongly pointed to HIV infection, which was confirmed by a positive HIV test. The rapid improvement after therapeutic pericardial aspiration and a full course of antituberculous treatment, corticosteroids, and antiretroviral therapy further confirms the diagnosis.
